title: Color 243 of 256-color palette is invisible in 8-color terminal
body:
Steps to reproduce: in Linux virtual console (`TERM=="linux"`) run
```
$ echo -e "Hello \e[38;5;243mWorld\e[0m."
```
The word `World` appears black on black, i.e. invisible.

[This commit](https://github.com/tmux/tmux/commit/37ad1e2f6da31ba8bf09865fccddec61addaad24) doesn't seem to fix the issue anymore. 

I tried to debug why it doesn't work with current code backported from obsd repo. It's weird but it looks like now [tty_attributes()](https://github.com/tmux/tmux/blob/36fba4cc54d543bec74a08597b89a019cb6edde3/tty.c#L2690) and subsequent [tty_check_fg()](https://github.com/tmux/tmux/blob/36fba4cc54d543bec74a08597b89a019cb6edde3/tty.c#L2845) aren't invoked at all.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
As I noted in the [original post](https://<redacted-host>/viewtopic.php?pid=2218759#p2218394), this is the coincidence of several factors:
1. linux always sets TERM to `linux` (even if it is actually true color framebuffer).
2. pacman uses color 243 for "faint" shade.
3. tmux maps color 243 to 8 if underlying terminal is not in 256 color mode first.
5. tmux maps color 8 to 0 if terminal supports only 8 colors according to terminfo.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
243 should be mapped to 0 (black) not 8 (default). Where do you see it end up as colour 8?

The problem here is that the default background is black and tmux does not know this in order to change the foreground colour to white like it does when you explicitly set a black background.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
> 243 should be mapped to 0 (black) not 8 (default). 

Em, "default" color in terms of ECMA-48 is `39`. In terms of attributes, color 8 is regular "dark grey", isn't it?

> Where do you see it end up as colour 8?

[colour.c:392](https://github.com/tmux/tmux/blob/f367e3a6c8761328b2233067b301909bb096d6fc/colour.c#L392), 4th element in last row.

> The problem here is that the default background is black and tmux does not know this in order to change the foreground colour to white like it does when you explicitly set a black background.

Does "default color" apply to cell attribute?

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
That 8 is only for the return value from `colour_256to16` and means "bright black" - it doesn't have any meaning beyond that. You can see in `tty_check_bg` this is converted immediately into one of tmux's actual colour representations - either 90 ("bright black") or 0 ("black").

But that's not what is happening here, and if I check the colours after `tty_check_bg` returns the colour is 8, which means default. If it was black it would be 90 or 0 and if it was the 256-colour-palette colour 8 it would be `COLOUR_FLAG_256|8` (`0x1000008`).

That's why tmux is sending this to the terminal:
~~~~
1745839641.728486 /dev/tty1: Hello
1745839641.728515 /dev/tty1: \033[30m
1745839641.728524 /dev/tty1: World
~~~~
It only changes the foreground colour to black (`\033[30m`) because the background is already the default colour so does not need to be changed.

Whereas if you add `\033[40m` to explicitly use black background instead of default, tmux will change the background too (and use a white foreground because now it can tell that foreground and background are both black):
~~~~
1745846170.614866 /dev/ttys007: Hello
1745846170.614936 /dev/ttys007: \033[37m
1745846170.614959 /dev/ttys007: \033[40m
1745846170.614981 /dev/ttys007: World
~~~~

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
So it seems it doesn't make sense to check background at all. At least tty_check_fg() behavior should not depend on whether it is called before tty_check_bg() or after.

I propose this PR https://github.com/tmux/tmux/pull/4495. Tested in linux virtual console with TERM=linux which has default black background and in xterm with TERM=xterm which has default white background. In both cases foreground color 243 is visible.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
I expect it is white on white without tmux because the default foreground is white and the SGR 38;5 sequence does nothing, not because the Linux console is mapping colour 243 to white.

I don't think we should replace one problem with another. Converting black-on-black or white-on-white to white-on-black or black-on-white is OK because it is obvious that nobody will want them, but we can't change all blacks into whites. We would need to know whether the default is black or white in order to make the correct decision.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
> I expect it is white on white without tmux because the default foreground is white 

But `033[38;5;243` changes foreground to 243 which is "shoehorned into 16 basic colors" ([sic](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man4/console_codes.4.html)), foreground is not default anymore.

>  and the SGR 38;5 sequence does nothing, not because the Linux console is mapping colour 243 to white.

Linux console maps 243 to RGB 0x767676 [here](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/f15d97df5afae16f40ecef942031235d1c6ba14f/drivers/tty/vt/vt.c#L1591) which turns into 7 with normal intensity [here](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/f15d97df5afae16f40ecef942031235d1c6ba14f/drivers/tty/vt/vt.c#L1612). 

> Converting black-on-black or white-on-white to white-on-black or black-on-white is OK because it is obvious that nobody will want them, but we can't change all blacks into whites. 

We don't change all blacks into whites. We change "something gray" into white instead of black in 8-color terminal. I don't know 8-color terminals with default white background (except, probably, ZX Spectrum :) ).

> We would need to know whether the default is black or white in order to make the correct decision.

I think heuristic is overhead here. "Something gray" must be mapped either into black or white when terminal can't display grey.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
If you want tmux to send 256 colours to Linux console and let it take care of it then you can configure it to do that.

If you don't, tmux will do the mapping and if the default background is black any colours that are mapped to black will be invisible and if the background is white any colours that are mapped to white will be invisible.

243 is closer to black so it is mapped to black and there are other greys closer to white that are mapped to white. If we make them all black or all white they will be wrong for someone.

I'm OK with automatically fixing obviously useless combinations like black-on-black and white-on-white but your change will make all greys white to to fix your particular problem and that is not OK.

The reason the default **background** (not the default foreground) matters is because if tmux knew whether it was black or white it could do the same automatic fix it does for when it knows the background is black.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
> 243 is closer to black so it is mapped to black and there are other greys closer to white that are mapped to white. 

Human eye sensitivity to brightness is not linear. One step between black and next grade looks more contrast than one step between white and previous grade. Mapping should take this into account, especially when converting to binary.

>  your change will make all greys white to to fix your particular problem and that is not OK.

Not all. 232..239 are still mapped to black (0).

comments.author: participant1
comments.body: No, your change makes every bright black foreground returned from `colour_256to16` white and we are not going to do that.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body: If you disagree with the mappings you need to change `colour_256to16` but you will need to show your reasoning.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
>232..239 are still mapped to black (0).

Typo, 232..237.

> No, your change makes every bright black foreground returned from `colour_256to16`

`colour_256to16()` returns 0 for 232..237, right? How it will go under `if (gc->fg & 8)` ? 

> If you disagree with the mappings you need to change colour_256to16

Mapping to **16** is ok. The problem arises with subsequent mapping 16 (4 grades) to 8 (2 grades).

comments.author: participant1
comments.body: Whichever way we go 16->8 (change bright black to black or to white) will be wrong for one of the two background colours.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body: Well, it's up to you whether to fix this issue or not. However, if PR https://github.com/tmux/tmux/pull/4495 is rejected, then https://github.com/tmux/tmux/commit/37ad1e2f6da31ba8bf09865fccddec61addaad24 should be reverted as well, I think.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
I don't think you understand the difference between the two changes.

37ad1e2 is converting black-on-black to white-on-black. This is always a good idea because black-on-black is never visible. This is an improvement for everyone.

Your new change is converting black-on-default to white-on-default. This is a good idea for you with a black background, but it is worse for anyone with a white background. So it fixes one case by breaking another. This is not an improvement.

So we are not going to make your change. If you want to do something about this there needs to be a better way, and I have suggested a few areas to look at:

- Work out what default background colour the terminal has. Maybe the Linux terminal has way to tell tmux? Or we could add a custom terminal capability to say. If tmux knew the background colour it could be sure that changing black-on-default to white-on-default would be the right thing to do.

- Adjust the colour mappings. You are right that vision is not linear, so is the mapping of greys to six black, six bright-black, six white, six bright-white correct? It you tweaked them maybe your problem would be fixed. What do other terminals do?

The other things I would look at it I was you:

- Does the Linux console really have no bright colours and no bold?

- Can you just run the problem application with 8 or 16 colours (`TERM=tmux` or a custom terminfo entry) so this isn't an issue for it?

- Or you could just keep a local change to tmux.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
> I don't think you understand the difference between the two changes.

I understand. I don't like two things there: 
- it's behavior relies on the order of `tty_check_fg()` / `tty_check_bg()` invocation
- it works only if application set background explicitly.

It was my misunderstanding of grid cell fields meaning.

> [37ad1e2](https://github.com/tmux/tmux/commit/37ad1e2f6da31ba8bf09865fccddec61addaad24) is converting black-on-black to white-on-black. This is always a good idea because black-on-black is never visible. This is an improvement for everyone.

In this case it is incomplete. It should also convert white-on-white into black-on-white.
However, if an application explicitly set black-on-black or white-on-white, no conversion should be performed, I believe.

>     * Work out what default background colour the terminal has. Maybe the Linux terminal has way to tell tmux? Or we could add a custom terminal capability to say. If tmux knew the background colour it could be sure that changing black-on-default to white-on-default would be the right thing to do.

I searched but didn't found relevant escape sequences or mentions in standards. Some software use `COLORFGBG` environment variable to detect "dark" or "light" scheme. However, it should be set by user and it is not standartized.

>     * Adjust the colour mappings. You are right that vision is not linear, so is the mapping of greys to six black, six bright-black, six white, six bright-white correct? It you tweaked them maybe your problem would be fixed. What do other terminals do?

GNU screen is displaying 243 as dark grey in linux terminal. I didn't research how they do this. However, GNU screen has many other issues.

>     * Does the Linux console really have no bright colours and no bold?

It has. Displaying bold as bright in terminal implementation is ok, as for me, but not the reverse. Applications should not assume that bold will always be treated as bright by terminal. However, many software do so. 

The problem would not arise if applications honor termcaps and don't assume that any terminal is 256-color capable. Unfortunately there are more and more such software. Some guys even put emojis into their official man pages.

>     * Can you just run the problem application with 8 or 16 colours (`TERM=tmux` or a custom terminfo entry) so this isn't an issue for it?

Personally I don't like agglomerations like
```
case ${TERM} in
  bla-bla-bla*) ... ;;
```
or similar constructions in shell profiles or aliases. 

>     * Or you could just keep a local change to tmux.

I already worked around the issue with
```
set -sa terminal-overrides "linux:colors=256"
```
in `tmux.conf` and added this into my personal long list of tips, tricks and workarounds.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body: OK it would be good to do white-on-white as well if we keep black-on-black but otherwise it seems like you have an acceptable workaround so I don't think we need to do anything else unless you want to add terminfo capabilities meaning "default background is black" or "white", but TBH I doubt anyone else would use them so it seems a bit overkill.
